newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma attacks Karen rebel camp, vows more raids.
newsitem.headline: Burma attacks Karen rebel camp, vows more raids.

text.p: Burma attacked a major ethnic Karen rebel camp on Friday and said it planned more raids until it had taken all Karen bases in the country, sources said.

Burmese soldiers attacked the Karen National Union's (KNU) camp, Htee Ka Per, in eastern Burmese jungle after overrunning three key KNU camps with motar and artillary fire earlier this week, Thai military sources said.
The fighting has driven over 20,000 Karen refugees into neighbouring Thailand. On Friday, Thai soldiers went on alert at the Burma border as refugees continued crossing into the country.

A Burmese government spokesman said raids on the rebels would continue and Burmese troops were determined to occupy any positions the KNU had set up inside the country. "This time, we will attack them and sit on any of their positions we take over," he told Reuters by telephone from the capital Rangoon.
The predominantly Christian rebels have fought the Burmese military government for greater autonomy for the Karen state since Burmese independence in 1948.
The refugees are now in two camps in the Thai border district of Umphang in Tak province, about four km (2.5 miles) from the Burmese border, the Thai military sources told Reuters.
The sources said about 400 Thai soldiers were on alert at the border area. "But so far there has been no fighting between Thai troops and Burmese soldiers," one military source said.
Burmese troops this week overran three key KNU mobile camps and dispersed about 4,000 KNU guerrillas and Karen living in the eastern jungle area.
Two Karens were wounded in Friday's fighting and sent to hospital in Thailand's Mae Sot district after being hit by mortar fire, the Thai military sources added.
But no casualty figures were available from either Karen or Burmese military officers.
In the latest round of fighting, the most serious between the Burmese and the Karen rebels since last year, the KNU have used hit-and-run tactics to attack Burmese soldiers.
Robert Htwe, chairman of the Karen Refugee Committee, on Friday urged the Thai govenment to respond swiftly to the refugees and ensure their safety.
"The camps where the refugees are living now are quite dangerous as they are located close to the border," he said.

Karen sources said the refugees now lived in fear because they were afraid of attacks by a rival KNU-splinter group, the Democratic Karen Buddhist Army (DKBA), which was backed by Rangoon and based inside Burma.
The DKBA split from the KNU in 1995 and has attacked refugees in camps along the Thai-Burma border.
About 70,000 ethnic Karen refugees, who fled earlier fighting inside Burma, have been living in sprawling refugee camps along Thailand's border for years.
The refugees are mostly family members and followers of the KNU. Thailand has promised to render humanitarian assistance to the displaced Karens.

U.K.-based Christian Aid, an organisation working with Karen refugees, said it was donating 50,000 sterling ($81,000) to the Burma Border Consortium to buy emergency food and supplies for the displaced Karen.

"The recent attacks underline the need for the international community to maintain its pressure for changes on the Burmese military government," the group's director, Michael Taylor, who this week visited the border area, said in a statement.
